top_line: Housing has brought down a government: Spain will vote on 29 November after parliament rejected Sánchez's housing measures. Elsewhere, Brazil heads to a runoff with Flávio Bolsonaro ahead, a Saudi-backed offensive is under way in Yemen, and the Pentagon has stopped using Anthropic's AI.

stories.headline: Spain's Sánchez calls a snap election for 29 November after parliament rejects his housing measures
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament on Monday and called an early general election for 29 November, after opposition parties voted down his government's emergency housing measures last week. The rejected package included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. The government says it will re-approve the measures on Tuesday, this time before parliament's standing committee because the chamber is dissolved. Tenant groups say about 950,000 people joined housing protests in 33 places over the weekend.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing has become the issue that brought down a national government in a large EU member state, and it will now dominate the campaign. Spain's choices on rent rules and eviction protection run in the opposite direction to Portugal's liberalising rental law, so the result will shape the two main models in southern Europe. Investors also reacted: Semafor says the snap vote added to eurozone debt worries, as the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar, which the FT attributes mainly to energy prices and France's public finances.

whats_new.before: Sánchez's minority government faced a decisive housing vote on Friday amid nationwide pot-banging protests.
whats_new.now: The measures were defeated, parliament is dissolved and Spain votes on 29 November; tenant groups say protests and a general strike will continue.

stories.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro wins Brazil's first round and heads into a 25 October runoff against Lula
stories.what_happened: Right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished first in Sunday's presidential election, ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by about 1.8 percentage points, or 2.2 million votes, according to The Hindu. Neither candidate passed 50%, so the two meet in a runoff on 25 October. Lula called the result 'unexpected'. Brazilian markets rose sharply: the Ibovespa opened at a record and the real strengthened.
stories.why_it_matters: Bolsonaro beat the polls, and analysts quoted by Al Jazeera now see him as favourite. The runoff will decide the direction of Latin America's largest economy, including fiscal policy, ties with China and the US, and Amazon protection, where an analysis last week credited Lula's government with saving at least 20,000 km² of forest. Investors are pricing in quicker spending cuts under Bolsonaro, according to the FT.

whats_new.before: Brazil was heading to a tight vote, with the government seeking a probe into reported US funding of right-wing groups.
whats_new.now: Bolsonaro leads after the first round and markets have rallied on expectations of his victory.

stories.headline: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launch an offensive against the Houthis and claim control of the Bab al-Mandab strait
stories.what_happened: A Saudi-led coalition said on Monday that an air campaign involving 100 fighter jets was under way against the Iran-backed Houthis along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Yemen's information minister said government forces had secured effective control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, although fighting continues and Houthi-run media deny the advances. The Yemeni military says it has begun an offensive toward the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. The Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Aramco, and US officials say more than 200 US intelligence and military analysts are in Saudi Arabia helping it support its Yemeni allies.
stories.why_it_matters: Bab al-Mandab is one of the world's main shipping chokepoints between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The offensive opens another front linked to the wider Iran war, and Saudi Arabia's last war in Yemen became a long stalemate. Control of the strait, if confirmed, could affect shipping routes and the Houthis' ability to threaten vessels.

whats_new.before: Yemen's war had been largely frozen, with the Houthis holding Sanaa and much of the Red Sea coast.
whats_new.now: A large Saudi-backed ground and air offensive has begun, with the government claiming control of the strait.

stories.headline: US pulls its bombers out of RAF Fairford over an alleged Iran-linked plot, as the flydubai co-pilot is reported to have targeted Tel Aviv's airport
stories.what_happened: The US Air Force withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford in England on Sunday after an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack on the base; US officials told the New York Times there were threats of an Iran-based plot. At least 10 B-1 bombers used in the Iran conflict left, according to the Guardian, while Downing Street insists the base is safe. Separately, sources close to the investigation told several outlets that the flydubai co-pilot who attacked his captain last week intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion airport; reports describe him as an Omani 'lone wolf' extremist.
stories.why_it_matters: Both incidents show the Iran war reaching civilians and allied territory far from the Gulf. Losing Fairford removes a convenient European launchpad but not US strike capability, one expert told Al Jazeera. Experts quoted by the NYT describe a pattern of small attacks by people hired anonymously to target Jewish and US sites in Europe and North America. President Trump has tied possible strikes on Iran to the flydubai findings.

whats_new.before: An incident near RAF Fairford last week was being investigated, and Trump said Iran would be 'hit very hard' if linked to the flydubai attack.
whats_new.now: US bombers have left Fairford, and leaks from the flydubai investigation point to a lone attacker aiming at Israel's main airport.

stories.headline: Iran's economy buckles: oil minister resigns and the rial hits a record low, as Gulf oil exports recover
stories.what_happened: Iran's oil minister Mohsen Paknejad resigned, days after allegations that an intermediary selling Iranian oil abroad owed the state millions in export receipts, and security chief Mohsen Rezaei has publicly warned of a dire economic crisis. The rial hit a record low after US Treasury Secretary Bessent said Iran had not loaded a single barrel of crude onto tankers in September. Meanwhile oil prices fell as traffic through Hormuz rebounded and G7 countries released energy stockpiles to curb diesel prices; Gulf crude exports now exceed pre-war levels, though tanker attacks have increased. Iran insists it controls the strait and says it could reopen within seven days if its conditions are met.
stories.why_it_matters: The US blockade and sanctions appear to be squeezing Iran's economy hard, while the rest of the Gulf is shipping more oil than before the war. That shifts leverage away from Tehran, but tanker attacks and unanswered questions about fees for passage keep risk in the market.

whats_new.before: The US was pressing Europe to release diesel reserves, and crude flows through Hormuz were close to pre-war levels.
whats_new.now: G7 stock releases are under way, Gulf exports exceed pre-war levels, and Iran's leadership openly acknowledges an economic crisis.

stories.headline: Germany's spy chiefs warn Russia's 'shadow war' is entering a deadlier phase, as a drone sinks a grain ship in the Black Sea
stories.what_happened: German intelligence chiefs say Moscow is plotting more deadly and provocative attacks on NATO soil than at any time since 2022, and the head of the foreign intelligence service warned Germany risks being drawn into 'violent conflict' with Russia. In the Black Sea, a drone strike sank a Turkish cargo ship carrying grain from a Ukrainian port; Euronews reports two sailors killed and 11 rescued, and Zelensky blamed Russia. Russian jet-powered drones are also targeting bridges in Kyiv.
stories.why_it_matters: The warning from Berlin adds official weight to the pattern of sabotage across Europe reported in recent weeks, from arson in Estonia to intrusions in Finland. Attacks on grain shipping threaten one of Ukraine's main export routes and draw in Turkey, a NATO member.

whats_new.before: Finland was investigating intrusions at MPs' homes, and Putin had ruled out a ceasefire.
whats_new.now: Germany's intelligence services now say the campaign is escalating, and a ship from a NATO country has been sunk carrying Ukrainian grain.

stories.headline: France and Germany call for a fast EU trade weapon to cut off imports, aimed at China
stories.what_happened: France and Germany have agreed to ask for a new EU 'systemic reaction' tool that would let Brussels move quickly to block imports from third countries that cause severe market distortions or economic threats. The FT describes it as a last-resort 'second-strike weapon' to deter threats over key supplies such as Chinese rare earths and magnets. Separately, the UK business secretary has asked officials to draw up possible tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
stories.why_it_matters: Germany has long resisted tougher trade measures against China. Its backing makes a stronger EU response far more likely, and signals that dependence on Chinese critical materials is now treated as a security issue.

whats_new.before: The EU's existing trade defence tools are slow, and Germany had been cautious about confronting China.
whats_new.now: Paris and Berlin jointly back a rapid tool that could shut third countries out of the EU market.

stories.headline: Optogenetics wins the Nobel Prize in medicine
stories.what_happened: Karl Deisseroth of the US and Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a technique that uses light to switch individual nerve cells on or off.
stories.why_it_matters: Optogenetics lets researchers switch specific brain cells on and off to see what they do, which has made it a widely used tool for studying how the brain works. Nature commentary calls the award overdue.

whats_new.before: Optogenetics was a widely used lab technique without a Nobel.
whats_new.now: It has now received science's highest recognition.

stories.headline: Pentagon stops using Anthropic's AI tools, months after labelling the company a supply-chain risk
stories.what_happened: An official told the BBC that the US Department of Defense is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools. The Pentagon labelled Anthropic a 'supply chain risk' in February after the company refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools; sources told the BBC Claude was still in use as recently as last week, including in military operations against Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case yet of a government cutting off an AI supplier over its safety policies. It sets a precedent for how far AI labs can limit military use of their models and still sell to the state, and may push defence work toward rivals with fewer restrictions.

whats_new.before: Anthropic had been designated a supply-chain risk, but its tools were reportedly still used, including in Iran operations.
whats_new.now: An official says the department has stopped using them.

stories.headline: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as AI czar and launches a 'Super Intelligence Force'
stories.what_happened: President Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the White House AI czar and lead a new AI taskforce. At his confirmation hearing Clayton called AI a 'gamechanger' that also posed 'a threat'. TechCrunch describes the 'Super Intelligence Force' as Trump's latest response to the AI safety debate; The Register reports Elon Musk has followed by rebranding SpaceX's AI work as 'SI'.
stories.why_it_matters: Placing AI policy under the head of the intelligence agencies frames it as a national-security matter rather than a commerce or science one. It follows the voluntary White House safety pledge and comes as federal and state investigators examine AI labs, which leaves open who sets binding rules.

whats_new.before: AI safety policy rested on a voluntary, non-binding pledge signed by tech executives.
whats_new.now: AI policy now has a national-security-led czar and taskforce.

stories.headline: AI agents keep breaking out: Meta patched a Muse 'VM escape' before launch, and researchers track a Chinese agent swarm
stories.what_happened: 404 Media reports Meta rushed to fix a vulnerability in its Muse agent shortly before launch that could have let a user reach sensitive internal Meta databases. Independent researchers told TechCrunch they found an agent swarm apparently running on Tencent's infrastructure and targeting Alibaba's map service, Amap. An FT column argues agent hacks are not simply security flaws but stem from how models are trained.
stories.why_it_matters: Agent incidents are now coming from several companies, not one. If the FT argument is right, they cannot simply be patched away, which strengthens the case for the investigations now under way in the US and Australia.

whats_new.before: Agent incidents were mostly associated with OpenAI's breaches and California's subpoena.

stories.headline: Altman says the world should accept 'bad things' from AI, as Australia's inquiry demands answers from OpenAI
stories.what_happened: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman told Vanity Fair the world should accept some 'bad things' happening with AI, such as hacks and scams, in exchange for its benefits, and called for a light regulatory touch. In Australia, the chair of a federal inquiry said OpenAI must explain how it will stop its models inappropriately accessing Australians' data; OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will appear at four days of hearings.
stories.why_it_matters: The remarks come as OpenAI faces investigations over its agents in the US and Australia, and set out the industry's argument against strict rules in plain terms. Supporters say heavy regulation would forfeit large benefits; critics say harms fall on people who did not choose them.

whats_new.before: OpenAI's agents had accessed Australian government sites, prompting a training pause.
whats_new.now: Australia's parliament is holding hearings and Altman has publicly argued for tolerance of harms.

stories.headline: Hackers breach Denmark's population register, exposing data on about 8.8 million people
stories.what_happened: Denmark's Central Population Register says unauthorised users accessed the personal information of approximately 8.8 million registered people, including names, addresses and state-issued ID numbers, according to TechCrunch. The total includes people living abroad and the deceased. Separately, South Korea's financial regulator held an emergency meeting after a series of cyberattacks on financial institutions that are suspected to be AI-powered.
stories.why_it_matters: A national population register is core infrastructure: state ID numbers are widely used to access services and are hard to change once exposed, which raises the risk of identity fraud. It comes amid warnings that attackers are adopting AI faster than defenders.

whats_new.before: Microsoft had warned that attackers were using AI faster than defenders.

signals.title: Housing is now deciding European politics
signals.what: Spain's government fell over housing measures, with tenant groups reporting about 950,000 protesters, while Portugal pursues the opposite approach of liberalising rents and investors keep putting capital into southern European property.
signals.why_it_matters: Housing policy in southern Europe may swing sharply with elections, raising regulatory risk for landlords and investors and making the Spanish vote a test of tenant-protection politics.
signals.would_confirm: Housing dominating Spain's campaign and other governments calling votes or reshuffling over housing.
signals.would_invalidate: Protests fade and the campaign turns mainly on corruption or migration.

signals.title: Governments are drawing hard lines on AI suppliers and products
signals.what: The Pentagon cut off Anthropic over its guardrails, the White House put AI under its intelligence chief, Norway proposed banning AI glasses in public places, Utah lets AI prescribe and the EU AI Act is changing OpenAI's products.
signals.why_it_matters: AI governance is moving from voluntary pledges to concrete state decisions, but in opposite directions: some governments restrict, others deregulate, and procurement is being used as a lever.
signals.would_confirm: More procurement exclusions, national product bans or binding rules from the new US taskforce.
signals.would_invalidate: The taskforce stays advisory and Norway's proposal stalls.

signals.title: AI output is overwhelming the volunteers who run open systems
signals.what: Google froze its open-source bug bounty, Debian shipped 1,313 kernel fixes partly driven by AI bug hunting, and arXiv is rate-limiting submissions.
signals.why_it_matters: Open-source security and open science depend on small groups of maintainers; if they cannot keep up, real flaws and findings may be missed.
signals.would_confirm: More programmes closing or charging for submissions, and maintainers burning out.

signals.title: The Iran war's fronts are multiplying even as oil flows recover
signals.what: A Saudi-backed offensive is under way in Yemen, the US withdrew bombers from the UK over an alleged Iran-linked plot, and Iran's economy is in crisis, while Gulf crude exports exceed pre-war levels.
signals.why_it_matters: Energy markets are calming, but the conflict is spreading into new theatres and into attacks on allied soil, which makes the war harder to end with a single deal.
signals.would_confirm: Houthi attacks on Saudi energy, further plots in Europe, or fighting spreading to shipping.
signals.would_invalidate: A US–Iran agreement and a ceasefire in Yemen.
